newsitem.title: USA: Former FDA chief critical of tobacco agreement.
newsitem.headline: Former FDA chief critical of tobacco agreement.

text.p: Former Food and Drug Administration chief David Kessler on Sunday criticized the deal between U.S. states and tobacco companies, saying major parts of the historic settlement need to be rewritten.
"I hope there is a resolution (of the tobacco issue). But not this one. Not the way it's written," Kessler said on NBC's "Meet The Press."

His comments were a blow to the agreement because he is an influential voice on U.S. health policy. Kessler was not involved in the negotiations, but he spearheaded President Bill Clinton's efforts to regulate tobacco as head of FDA. The White House has said it would consult him before deciding whether to support the settlement.
The agreement calls for the industry to pay $368.5 billion over 25 years in part to fund major new anti-smoking efforts. In return, the industry gets some protection from legal liability.

But Kessler made clear that he sees another key part of agreement -- touted by the state attorneys general at a high-profile announcement on Friday as giving the FDA the power to regulate and eventually ban nicotine in cigarettes -- as less than meets the eye.
"The settlement could effectively impede FDA's ability to regulate ... tobacco products," Kessler said. "There are a lot of hurdles for the FDA, some impossible burdens."
"This document has a lot of legal terms and ... this seems to be a step back," he said.

Kessler did not elaborate. But the agreement would give the FDA the power to eliminate nicotine only after 12 years and said the FDA would have to prove that reductions in nicotine levels would lead to health improvements.
It also said the FDA would have to show that reducing levels of nicotine in cigarettes would not lead to a black market in high-nicotine cigarettes.
"I'd like to see a resolution and I certainly support some of the elements but other elements have to be rewritten," Kessler said of the settlement.
"This settlement is asking the industry to do something it would not naturally do -- sell fewer cigarettes to people. And if you look at the penalties, I don't think they're strong enough," he said.
The FDA believes it already has the jurisdiction to regulate cigarettes and smokeless tobacco as drugs and has issued new rules barring teenagers from buying tobacco products.
A federal court in Greensboro, North Carolina upheld the rules dealing with sales to minors in a suit filed against FDA by the tobacco industry. The industry appealed that ruling.

Even before the landmark settlement was announced on Friday, the FDA was planning to move ahead with enforcing rules curbing teenage use of tobacco, and with restrictions on advertising as soon as possible, Associate FDA Commissioner Mitch Zeller told Reuters.

Zeller, who was leading the FDA tobacco effort, said the agency does not have to wait for any industry-government agreement to give it more power. Just last week, the agency signed the first contract, with the state of Florida, to enforce the provision barring minors under age 18 from buying cigarettes.

Another contract was due to be signed soon, and the agency hoped to have 10 states on board by October. Zeller said the agency aims to get enough money from Congress to hire agents in all 50 states to enforce the rules. FDA asked for $34 million for tobacco control for fiscal year 1998.
